title: The Flood at the China-Nepal Border
author: Ed Rush

slides.title: The flood at the China-Nepal border
slides.body: What happened? Why? What can we do?
slides.notes: Point at the flood image. Ask: Where is this? What do you see?

slides.title: Why is this lesson important?
slides.body:
• This flood shows how a small event can become a disaster.
  • Floods are a real risk across Asia, including Thailand.
  • You will practise talking about climate change in English.

slides.title: Listen and write the questions
slides.body:
You will hear eight questions.
Write each question. You will hear each one twice.

Dictation tape
slides.notes: Play the dictation tape. Students write the 8 questions as they hear them. Play twice.

slides.title: Check your dictation — Part 1
slides.body:
Emma says the flood was not a normal flood. What was it like, and why was it so dangerous?

Why was the loud noise so surprising to the people in Nuwakot?
slides.notes: Read the two questions aloud. Students tick or correct what they wrote.

slides.title: Check your dictation — Part 2
slides.body:
Why did so many people first believe that there had been an earthquake?

Why is it so hard for scientists to warn people before a glacier collapses?
slides.notes: Read the two questions aloud. Students tick or correct what they wrote.

slides.title: Check your dictation — Part 3
slides.body:
Give two examples of the damage that the flood caused to buildings and infrastructure.

How many people were affected in total, and around how many children lost their classrooms?
slides.notes: Read the two questions aloud. Students tick or correct what they wrote.

slides.title: Check your dictation — Part 4
slides.body:
Emma says the danger is not over. Why?

Why does Emma think that this is a climate story, and not only a Nepal story?
slides.notes: Read the two questions aloud. Students tick or correct what they wrote.

slides.title: Answers — Part 1
slides.body:
QuestionWhat was the flood like, and why was it so dangerous?
AnswerIt was a wall of water, mud, rocks and broken ice. It moved incredibly fast, so people had no time to run.
QuestionWhy was the loud noise so surprising?
AnswerIt sounded like thunder, but the sky was clear and blue, with no clouds.
slides.notes: Read each question, ask students, then reveal the answer.

slides.title: Answers — Part 2
slides.body:
QuestionWhy did many people first think it was an earthquake?
AnswerThe US Geological Survey recorded a small tremor, about 4.4. So people thought the earthquake had caused a landslide.
QuestionWhy is it so hard to warn people before a glacier collapses?
AnswerThe Himalayas are huge and remote, and the weather was calm that day. There are thousands of glaciers, so scientists cannot say which one will break, or when.
slides.notes: Read each question, ask students, then reveal the answer.

slides.title: Answers — Part 3
slides.body:
QuestionGive two examples of damage to buildings and infrastructure.
AnswerIt destroyed homes, roads and bridges. It also blocked the tunnels of hydroelectric power stations.
QuestionHow many people were affected? How many children lost classrooms?
AnswerAbout 65,000 people were affected. Around 10,000 children lost their classrooms.
slides.notes: Read each question, ask students, then reveal the answer.

slides.title: Answers — Part 4
slides.body:
QuestionWhy is the danger not over?
AnswerA barrier lake has formed behind rocks and debris. Water is building up, and if it breaks, there could be a second flood.
QuestionWhy is this a climate story, not only a Nepal story?
AnswerThe warming planet makes flooding worse across Asia. Thailand is also at risk, and countries like Nepal cause little of the problem but feel it first.
slides.notes: Read each question, ask students, then reveal the answer.

slides.title: A speaking card
slides.body:
|||

Work with a partner. Use the card structure.

Open — start the talk.

Opinion — say what you think.

Reason — give a reason.

Agree or disagree — reply to your partner.

Agreement — find a compromise.
slides.notes: Walk through the 5-step structure on the card. Model one short example with a student.

slides.title: Strategy: Close the discussion
slides.body:
DoEnd the talk by saying the compromise you both accept.
WhyA clear resolution shows you understood and agreed.
HowSay the middle point. Then say: "So, can we compromise and say ...?"
slides.notes: Teach the ENDING. Summarise the middle point, then state the resolution both partners accept. One closing sentence each.

slides.title: Card 1 — the resolution
slides.body:
Card 1: Is climate change mainly caused by people?

Partner A"I think people cause climate change."
Partner B"I see your point, but nature also changes the weather."
Resolution"So, can we compromise and say people and nature both play a part?"
slides.notes: Model the END of the discussion — the resolution. Partner A vs B, then both state the final compromise. Students repeat the 'So, can we compromise and say...?' pattern.

slides.title: Resolution — closing the discussion
slides.body:
State the agreement: "So, can we compromise and say ... ?"

Or: "Could we agree that ... ?" "Maybe we can both ..."

Confirm: "So we both think ..., right?"

Close: "Great, we agree on that."
slides.notes: Step 5 endings — these close the discussion. One resolution statement that both partners say together.

slides.title: Speed dating — Card Set A
slides.body:
Pair up. One card each. Discuss for 2 minutes.

Use the structure and the language on the card. Then move to the next partner.
slides.notes: Set A = structured cards with language support. 2-minute rounds. Rotate partners.

slides.title: Speed dating — Card Set B
slides.body:
Now no language help. Talk for 2 minutes.

Use your own ideas. Then move to the next partner.
slides.notes: Set B = bare cards, no language support. Students must use the structure on their own.
